prompt: Ana has an uncommitted edit to `main.tf` and runs `terraform plan`. What does the plan describe?
hint: Look at what `git status` printed before the plan.

choices.text: The last commit on her branch
choices.why: Terraform does not ask git anything; it read the edited file on disk.

choices.text: The files as they are on disk
choices.why: Yes. The new range appeared in the plan although no commit contained it.

choices.text: Whatever is on `main` in the remote repository
choices.why: Terraform never reads the remote; that is the pipeline's clone doing it.

choices.text: Nothing until the edit is committed, since Terraform refuses a dirty tree
choices.why: There is no such refusal; the capture shows a full plan from a dirty tree.

prompt: The diff of Ana's change is one line. Why does the lesson say a reviewer needs the plan as well?
hint: What did that one line do to the subnet?

choices.text: A one-line diff is too short to review
choices.why: Its length is not the problem; its consequence is invisible in it.

choices.text: The plan shows that the line replaces the subnet, which the diff does not say
choices.why: Right: `# forces replacement`, one to add and one to destroy, from a range change.

choices.text: Reviewers cannot read HCL
choices.why: They can; the point is what the HCL causes, which only a plan computes.

choices.text: The plan is required by GitHub before a merge
choices.why: GitHub knows nothing about Terraform; the pipeline posts the plan because people need it.

prompt: Which of these does moving the apply from laptops into one pipeline change? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section's table has three rows.

choices.text: Which Terraform version applies
choices.why: Yes: one version, written in the workflow.

choices.text: Where credentials that can write live
choices.why: Yes: in one place, for one job, instead of on every laptop.

choices.text: Whether the change is a wise one
choices.why: People still decide that; the pipeline only does the mechanical part.

choices.text: Whether there is a record of each apply and its commit
choices.why: Yes: a log per run, tied to a commit and an approval.

choices.text: Whether Terraform needs a state
choices.why: It needs one wherever it runs; the pipeline uses the same S3 state.

prompt: Put the pipeline's steps on `main` in order, from the merge to the change being made.
hint: The file has to exist before anybody can read it.
items: the file kept as an artifact
a person reads and approves it
trap: Approving before the plan is saved approves something that can still change.

prompt: In the lesson's pipeline, why do `check` and `scan` run before `plan`?
hint: Compare what each step needs.

choices.text: Terraform refuses to plan unformatted code
choices.why: It plans it happily; `fmt -check` is a rule the pipeline adds.

choices.text: A plan writes to the cloud, so it has to be last but one
choices.why: A plan writes nothing in the cloud; it reads, and locks the state.

choices.text: They are cheap and need no credentials
choices.why: Yes. A failure there costs seconds and no credential was ever handed out.

choices.text: The scanner reads the plan file
choices.why: Here Trivy reads the `.tf` files; scanning a plan is lesson 14's subject.

prompt: The pull request already has a plan the reviewers read. Why is another plan made on `main` after the merge?
hint: Two pull requests approved on the same morning.

choices.text: It goes stale once anything else lands on `main`
choices.why: Right. The pull request's plan is true for the state it read; the applied one must be made from `main` as it is.

choices.text: A pull request's plan cannot be saved
choices.why: It could be; it is not applied because it goes stale, not because of a limit.

choices.text: To use the apply role
choices.why: The plan on `main` runs with the read-only plan role too.

choices.text: Terraform plans each branch into a different state
choices.why: Both read the same state key in the bucket.

prompt: In the capture, what made the pipeline stop on the pull request that opened port 22?
hint: Look at the last line of the capture.

choices.text: `terraform validate` rejected the rule
choices.why: `check` passed: the file was valid HCL.

choices.text: Trivy's non-zero exit code
choices.why: Yes. `--exit-code 1` turns a HIGH finding into a failed step, and a failed step ends the job.

choices.text: The plan showed a security group being replaced
choices.why: No plan ran at all; the scan stopped the pipeline first.

choices.text: AWS refused the rule when the pipeline tried to create it
choices.why: Nothing reached AWS; the scan reads files and needs no credentials.

prompt: Why does the workflow write `actions/checkout@3d3c42e…` instead of `actions/checkout@v7`?
hint: Which of the two can the action's owner change?

choices.text: A tag is movable; a commit is not
choices.why: Right. Whatever the tag points at runs with your credentials, so the pin is the commit.

choices.text: GitHub no longer accepts tags in `uses`
choices.why: It accepts them; the choice is about trust, not syntax.

choices.text: It downloads faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: So that Dependabot cannot update the action
choices.why: Pins can still be updated, deliberately; the comment with the tag is there to make that readable.

prompt: Why does every step in the workflow call `ci.sh` instead of listing the Terraform commands itself?
hint: Think about the GitLab file and Ana's laptop.

choices.text: GitHub cannot run more than one command per step
choices.why: A `run:` block can hold many lines; the comment step in this workflow has two.

choices.text: Shell scripts run faster than YAML steps
choices.why: Both run the same commands in the same shell.

choices.text: To hide the commands from people reading the logs
choices.why: The opposite: `set -x` prints every command into the log.

choices.text: The steps are written once and run the same anywhere
choices.why: Yes: GitHub, GitLab and a laptop run the same stages, which is also how this lesson ran them.

prompt: Without a flag, a missing variable makes Terraform wait for an answer at `Enter a value:`. The flag that turns that question into an immediate error is `-input=___`.
hint: A boolean.

prompt: What does setting `TF_IN_AUTOMATION` change in the capture?
hint: Compare the last lines of the two plans.

choices.text: It skips the confirmation question of `apply`
choices.why: That is `-auto-approve`, or applying a saved plan; the variable only changes wording.

choices.text: It makes Terraform fail when input would be needed
choices.why: That is `-input=false`; the lesson shows both because they are easy to confuse.

choices.text: Advice meant for a person at a keyboard disappears
choices.why: Yes. The note about `-out` and the hint to run `terraform apply "tfplan"` are left out.

choices.text: Colour codes are removed from the output
choices.why: Colour is `-no-color`; the variable leaves it alone.

prompt: Match each job of the design to the GitLab keyword that does it.
hint: Look at the table that compares the two dialects.

pairs.left: Carry the plan's file to a later job
Stop until a person presses a button
Only one apply at a time
A token for AWS without a stored key

prompt: Why does the lesson call `expire_in: 3 days` on the plan artifact a decision rather than housekeeping?
hint: What else is inside a saved plan?

choices.text: GitLab charges for every day an artifact is kept
choices.why: Cost is not the argument the lesson makes.

choices.text: Terraform refuses plans older than three days
choices.why: Terraform checks the state's serial, not the file's age.

choices.text: The file holds a copy of the state
choices.why: Right. Keeping it longer keeps that copy downloadable for longer, for a plan that has waited so long it should be made again rather than applied.

choices.text: Artifacts older than that are deleted from the state bucket
choices.why: Artifacts live in GitLab, not in the state bucket.

prompt: What did the lab check about the two workflow files?
hint: Look at the `python3` commands.

choices.text: Valid YAML, with the expected jobs
choices.why: Yes, and the lesson says how little that proves.

choices.text: That they run on GitHub and GitLab
choices.why: The lab has neither; the files were never run.

choices.text: That every action and image exists
choices.why: Nothing in the lab reached GitHub or a registry.

choices.text: That the OIDC exchange works
choices.why: Only a real run would show the exchange; moto would accept any token anyway.

prompt: What is wrong with an IAM user's access key stored in the repository's secrets?
hint: How long does it work, and from where?

choices.text: GitHub refuses secrets longer than 40 characters
choices.why: There is no such limit in play here.

choices.text: It lives until rotated and works from anywhere
choices.why: Right. One leak and it is somebody else's for as long as nobody notices.

choices.text: Terraform cannot read keys from environment variables
choices.why: It can; that is why the shortcut works on the first try.

choices.text: Access keys cannot apply, only plan
choices.why: A key can do whatever its user may do, which is the problem.

prompt: The apply role's trust policy matches `sub` to `repo:example/shop:environment:production`. What does that buy?
hint: Which jobs enter that environment?

choices.text: Only jobs of the `main` branch may plan
choices.why: Planning uses the other role, which trusts pull requests too.

choices.text: The token never expires while the environment exists
choices.why: The credentials expire within the hour regardless.

choices.text: Write access only after approval
choices.why: Yes. A job enters `production` only once approved, so the approval and the credential are one gate.

choices.text: Moto refuses tokens from any other repository
choices.why: Moto evaluates no trust policy at all; the lesson says so.

prompt: A colleague removes `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` from the plan role, to make it truly read-only. What happens to the next plan?
hint: `use_lockfile = true` is in `backend.tf`.

choices.text: It fails, because it cannot write the lock file
choices.why: Right. A plan locks the state, and with `use_lockfile` the lock is an object written beside it.

choices.text: It runs, since a plan only reads
choices.why: It reads the cloud, but it also takes the state lock, which is a write to the bucket.

choices.text: It runs without a lock and prints a warning
choices.why: Terraform does not skip the lock on its own; it fails to acquire it.

choices.text: It runs, but cannot read the state any more
choices.why: Reading the state is `s3:GetObject`, which stays.

prompt: Why should the plan role be able to read and nothing more? Choose all that apply.
hint: Whose code does a plan on a pull request run?

choices.text: Providers execute code during a plan
choices.why: Yes, so a plan is not a passive read.

choices.text: A data source such as `external` runs a program the configuration names
choices.why: Yes, and the configuration comes from whoever opened the pull request.

choices.text: Reading the state needs the `ReadOnlyAccess` policy
choices.why: `s3:GetObject` on the key is enough; the lab wrote it out.

choices.text: Whoever can open a pull request can make the plan act with that role
choices.why: Yes, which is why its credentials must be worth little.

choices.text: A plan role that can write is refused by AWS
choices.why: AWS will happily issue it; the restraint is yours to write.

prompt: Run 1's apply job ran in a clone whose `main.tf` asked for an `Owner` tag. The VPC it created has none. Why?
hint: What does a saved plan carry?

choices.text: Moto drops tags it does not know
choices.why: Moto kept `Name` and `Environment`; the plan never asked for `Owner`.

choices.text: `init` reverted the file to the plan's commit
choices.why: `init` touches no `.tf` file; `grep` still found `Owner` afterwards.

choices.text: The plan holds its own configuration
choices.why: Right. `apply tfplan` carries out what was computed and approved, not what the files around it say now.

choices.text: Tags are applied by a second run of `apply`
choices.why: Tags are ordinary arguments; the tag came later through run 2's own plan.

prompt: Why must the apply job on `main` not run `terraform apply -auto-approve`?
hint: What would it apply?

choices.text: It plans again and applies a plan nobody read
choices.why: Yes: the approval would be for one plan and the apply for another.

choices.text: `-auto-approve` is not allowed with an S3 backend
choices.why: It is allowed; the lessons used it on the S3 backend.

choices.text: It ignores the state lock
choices.why: It takes the lock like any apply.

choices.text: It needs a terminal to show the plan
choices.why: It prints the plan to the log, which nobody approved.

prompt: The plan artifact expired before anybody approved the run. What should the pipeline do?
hint: A plan is a statement about one moment.

choices.text: Apply without a plan file, since the code was reviewed
choices.why: That is the fallback the lesson forbids: it applies a plan nobody read.

choices.text: Run the plan job again and have that plan read
choices.why: Right. Expiry, like staleness, means plan again and read again.

choices.text: Raise `retention-days` and re-run only the apply job
choices.why: The file is already gone; a longer retention cannot bring it back.

choices.text: Copy `tfplan` from a laptop
choices.why: That would apply a file no reviewer saw, made by a laptop the pipeline replaced.

prompt: Run 2 planned while run 1 was waiting for approval. How many resources did run 2's first plan propose to add?
hint: Its `Plan:` line.

prompt: The state lock from lesson 7 was in place the whole time. Why did run 2 still plan against a state that was about to change?
hint: When is the lock held, and for how long?

choices.text: The lock only covers `apply`
choices.why: A plan takes the lock too, as the plan role's permissions showed.

choices.text: A lock only stops two operations at the same instant
choices.why: Right. Each plan held it briefly; nothing stopped the second plan once the first had finished planning.

choices.text: `-lock-timeout=5m` disabled the lock
choices.why: It makes Terraform wait for a lock, not skip it.

choices.text: The two runs used different state keys
choices.why: Both used `shop/terraform.tfstate`; that is why run 2 went stale.

prompt: Why is `cancel-in-progress` set to `false` in the workflow's `concurrency` block?
hint: What happens to an apply cancelled halfway?

choices.text: So that pull requests are never cancelled
choices.why: The setting is about the running job of the group, whatever its event.

choices.text: GitHub requires it when `environment` is used
choices.why: There is no such requirement; it is a choice about safety.

choices.text: To keep every pending run in the queue
choices.why: Pending runs are still replaced by newer ones; this only protects the running one.

choices.text: A cancelled apply is a partial apply
choices.why: Yes: lesson 9's partial apply, made on purpose.

prompt: A team keeps the GitHub workflow but changes the `apply` job's checkout to `ref: main`. Two merges land minutes apart. What is the risk?
hint: What does the apply job read from the checkout, and what from the plan?

choices.text: The plan file is ignored and the newer commit is applied
choices.why: `apply tfplan` follows the plan, as the lesson's run 1 showed.

choices.text: A lock file from another commit
choices.why: Right. `init` reads the backend and the lock file from the checkout, and a plan whose provider selections differ is refused.

choices.text: Both commits are applied twice
choices.why: Each run applies its own plan once; the second may go stale.

choices.text: None: the checkout does not matter to `apply tfplan`
choices.why: The configuration comes from the plan, but the backend and the lock file come from the checkout.

prompt: A team wants a faster pipeline and proposes: on a merge, run `terraform apply -auto-approve` on `main`, since the pull request's plan was already reviewed. Which run in this lesson shows the flaw?
hint: Which plan was true when made and false later?

choices.text: The pull request that opened port 22
choices.why: The scan stopped that one before any plan; it says nothing about reviewing plans.

choices.text: Run 2, whose plan proposed a second network
choices.why: Right. What was reviewed was no longer what would happen; with `-auto-approve` the apply would have planned afresh and nobody would have read that plan either.

choices.text: Ana's uncommitted subnet change on her laptop
choices.why: That shows why laptops should not apply, not why a merged change needs a fresh, read plan.

choices.text: The `ci-roles` configuration
choices.why: That is the credentials, applied once by an administrator.

prompt: Ana's company moves from GitHub to GitLab. Which of these must change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what schedules the steps from what the steps are.

choices.text: `ci.sh`
choices.why: Both files call the same script; that is why it exists.

choices.text: The file that schedules the jobs
choices.why: Yes: `.gitlab-ci.yml` instead of the workflow.

choices.text: The OIDC provider and the `sub` conditions in AWS
choices.why: Yes: the issuer becomes `https://gitlab.com` and `sub` has GitLab's shape.

choices.text: The S3 backend and its lock file
choices.why: The state does not care which CI service plans against it.

choices.text: The Terraform configuration of the network
choices.why: The network is the same whatever runs the pipeline.
